🫙 Cooking, drying and storing - Cook all wild mushrooms — never raw, and morels especially well done. Don't mix alcohol with morels the first time (some people react). - Dry slices about ½ inch thick at about 120 °F with good airflow until crisp; morels lose about 90% of their weight. Store airtight. Rehydrate in hot water. Ventilate while drying — spores can trigger asthma. (OSU SP 50-919; USFS PNW-GTR-710) - Freeze after sautéing (best) or steam-blanching. - Never can wild mushrooms — only store-type button mushrooms have tested canning times.

🪵 Growing your own - Shiitake on logs: fresh hardwood logs (oak is among the best) 4–6 inches across, cut in the dormant season while the bark is tight. Drill holes 7/16 inch wide, 1¼ inches deep, 3 inches apart in a diamond pattern, plug with spawn, seal with wax. Keep shaded and moist. Mushrooms start in 6–18 months; after that, soak a log 24 hours and it fruits about a week later. Rest logs 8–12 weeks between soaks. (UVM/Cornell; USDA Agroforestry Note 13) - Oysters on straw: chop straw 4–5 inches, soak overnight, pasteurize at 165 °F for 1–2 hours, mix in 5–10% spawn, pack into bags with holes, keep warm and humid. Fruits in weeks. (UF IFAS SS662) - Keep your strain going: a piece of a fruiting log or colonized straw can start the next batch, so you don't need to buy spawn again.

🌿 Medicinal mushrooms Turkey tail, reishi, lion's mane and shiitake have real research behind them as add-ons to treatment — turkey-tail extract (PSK) is a prescribed cancer add-on in Japan — but most evidence is from lab and animal studies. They are not cures. Turkey tail and reishi are traditionally simmered for hours as tea. (VA Mycomedicinals)The old mushroom books here (1895–1928) are great for pictures, descriptions and recipes, but some of their safety advice is wrong and has killed people: Marshall's Mushroom Book lists false morels as edible, Thomas says the parasol has no poisonous look-alike, and USDA FB 796 recommends raw mushrooms and old first aid. They also miss most western killers. Use the modern files in Poisoning-Safety and this guide for anything about safety.

☢️ Nuclear Fallout Guide What to do if there is a nuclear detonation or a radiation release: how to shelter, how long, how to protect food, water and animals, how to clean up, and when potassium iodide (KI) helps. The full manuals — shelter plans, the homemade KFM fallout meter, farm and livestock guides — are in Nuclear-Radiation\. ### The three rules 1. Get inside. Stay inside. Stay tuned. Most deaths from fallout are avoidable just by being behind enough mass in the first day or two. 2. Fallout is dust. It hurts you from what lands on and near you, so put mass and distance between you and the roof, walls and ground outside. 3. Time is on your side. Radiation from fallout drops fast — 90% in the first 7 hours, 99% in 2 days.

⚡ The first minutes - If you see a flash: drop behind anything solid, face down, cover your head, and don't look at it. The blast wave can arrive many seconds later — stay down until it passes. - Fallout near a blast can start arriving in 15–30 minutes; 100–200 miles downwind, often 5–10 hours or more. Use the time before it arrives to put out small fires, bring people, pets and water inside, and move to the best shelter you can reach. (FEMA Protection in the Nuclear Age, H-20) - Officials will tell everyone within about 50 miles to shelter until they know where the fallout is going. (FEMA Planning Guidance, 3rd ed.)

🏠 Where to shelter Best to worst: a basement (especially a corner below ground level) → the middle floors and center of a large concrete or brick building → a crawl space or interior room of a house → a vehicle (poor). Most homes in the Illinois Valley are one-story wood frame with no basement. FEMA says these, and vehicles, are not adequate shelter on their own. Plan now: a nearby building with a basement or thick masonry, a crawl-space shelter you can shield, or an outdoor trench shelter (plans in MP-79, In Time of Emergency, and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix A). - Inside any building: get as far from the roof and outside walls as you can, away from windows and doors. Close and lock windows, turn off fans, A/C and forced-air heat, close fireplace dampers. (CDC Where to Go) - Stuck in a poor shelter? If a good one is under 15 minutes away, move within about 30 minutes of the blast, before heavy fallout arrives. If you're already in a moderate shelter, stay 1–2 hours, then move. (FEMA Planning Guidance) Adding shielding — each of these stops about as much as 4 inches of concrete (FEMA H-20): | Material | Thickness | | Brick | 5–6 in | | Sand or gravel | 6 in | | Packed earth | 7 in | | Hollow concrete

H-20): | Material | Thickness | | Brick | 5–6 in | | Sand or gravel | 6 in | | Packed earth | 7 in | | Hollow concrete block (sand-filled) | 8 in (6 in) | | Water | 10 in | | Books or magazines | 14 in | | Wood (firewood stack) | 18 in | Pile it on the floor above you and around the walls of your shelter spot: earth-filled drawers and boxes, water jugs, firewood, books, heavy furniture. Every extra ~4 inches of packed earth roughly halves what gets through — about 3 feet of earth cuts it around 1,000×. Crawl space: shelter under the center of the house, ring yourself with blocks or earth-filled containers, and pile mass on the floor above. Ventilation: a crowded, sealed shelter gets dangerously hot in warm weather. Kearny's homemade air pump (KAP) — plans in Nuclear War Survival Skills and the ORNL Expedient Shelter Handbook — moves air without bringing in fallout dust.

⏳ How long to stay in The 7-10 rule: every 7× increase in time after the blast cuts the radiation 10× (once the fallout has finished falling). | Time after blast | Radiation level (example) | | 1 hour | 1,000 R/hr | | 7 hours | 100 R/hr | | 2 days | 10 R/hr | | 2 weeks | 1 R/hr | - Stay sheltered at least 12–24 hours (FEMA). In heavy fallout areas it can be several days to two weeks, with only short trips out once levels drop (H-20). - Without a meter, listen for official word. With a meter, you can make your own decisions — see below.

🧼 Cleaning yourself up (decontamination) (CDC; EPA Protective Action Q&A) - Taking off your outer layer of clothes removes up to 90% of the fallout on you. Do it before you enter the shelter if you can. Bag the clothes and put them away from people and pets. - Shower with soap and shampoo — no conditioner (it glues particles to hair). Don't scrub hard or scratch the skin; keep cuts covered. - No shower? Wipe exposed skin, blow your nose, wipe eyelids, ears and face with a damp cloth. - Clothes from closed drawers and closets are fine to wear. - Pets: bring them in. Wash with soap or shampoo and water, wearing gloves and a dust mask, rinse completely, then wash yourself. - Fallout looks like sand, ash or grit. Brush or hose it off roofs and away from the house after levels drop; wear a dust mask, gloves and a hat, and wash afterward.

💊 Potassium iodide (KI) - KI only protects the thyroid, and only from radioactive iodine. It does nothing against other fallout. Take it only when health officials say to — or, with no officials, when you have reason to believe fresh fallout or a reactor plume is arriving. Table salt and iodine tincture are not substitutes (tincture is poisonous to swallow). (CDC; FDA) - One dose protects about 24 hours. It works best just before or as the plume arrives and still helps 3–4 hours after. Avoid repeat doses for newborns and pregnant or breastfeeding women. (FDA) FDA dose by age (one dose per day): | Who | Dose | | Adults over 18 (including pregnant or breastfeeding) | 130 mg | | Ages 12–18 (130 mg if 154 lb or more) | 65 mg | | Ages 3–12 | 65 mg | | 1 month – 3 years | 32 mg | | Birth – 1 month | 16 mg | Adults over 40 need it only for a very large expected exposure. To make liquid doses for small children from tablets, use the two FDA sheets in Nuclear-Radiation\Government-Guidance.

🥫 Food and water (EPA Protective Action Q&A; FDA; Nuclear War Survival Skills Ch. 8) - Food that was indoors is fine. Sealed cans, jars and bags that were outside are fine after wiping the outside. Stored grain and canned food have no radioactive-iodine risk. - Don't eat garden produce or anything left uncovered outdoors until levels have dropped and it's declared clear — then wash and peel it. - Don't drink fresh milk from animals grazing fallout-covered pasture for the first weeks (radioactive iodine concentrates in milk). Milk made into cheese and aged two months or more is fine — the radioactive iodine decays away. - Water: bottled and sealed water is certain. Covered wells, tanks and cisterns are the best sources; deep wells are well protected. Tap water is fine for washing. - Boiling does not remove radioactivity. To clean doubtful water: stir in clay soil, let it settle several hours, and pour off the clear water — or filter it through a bucket of packed earth. Both remove most fallout particles. Then disinfect as usual. - Cover rain barrels, tanks and well heads ahead of time.

🐄 Livestock and gardens (USDA FB 2107, PA-516; Oregon ODOE) - Shelter animals if you can (a barn helps), and take them off pasture. Feed protected feed — hay from inside the stack, covered silage, grain from closed bins. - Water from a covered well, tank or flowing spring is best; open pond water clears more slowly but improves quickly. - Hold off on slaughter, fresh milk and eggs until levels drop. - Gardens: stop harvesting; after levels drop, wash and peel produce. Fallout on soil decays and is diluted by digging it in.

📟 Measuring radiation - A meter turns guessing into decisions — when to leave the shelter, which room is safest, whether the water is clear. - KFM (Kearny Fallout Meter): a homemade meter from a can, foil and paper. Build it before you need it. The patterns must print exactly to scale — check against a ruler; OISM warns online copies of the templates aren't fully reliable and recommends the printed book. Full patterns and tables: ORNL-5040 and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix C. - Old civil-defense meters turn up at sales: the yellow CD V-715 reads high levels (fallout); the CD V-700 is a low-range Geiger counter for checking food, water and people. Manuals and a home-study course are in Nuclear-Radiation\Measuring-Radiation.

📍 Our area - The region's only operating nuclear power plant is the Columbia Generating Station at Hanford, Washington — roughly 350 miles from the Illinois Valley, far outside its planning zones. (Oregon ODOE) - The more realistic threats here are fallout drifting from detonations elsewhere and fallout carried across the Pacific on west winds. After Chernobyl, radioactive iodine showed up in milk in northwest Oregon. (Nuclear War Survival Skills) - OISM, publisher of Nuclear War Survival Skills, is in Cave Junction — the printed edition (with accurate KFM patterns) may be easy to get locally.The 1987 edition of Nuclear War Survival Skills includes the author's personal view that small radiation doses are healthful; FEMA, EPA and CDC do not accept that. Follow the government guidance in this folder for dose decisions.

🔧 Engines, Motors and Generators How to keep small gas engines, chainsaws and generators running, how to test and rebuild electric motors, and how to turn motors and car alternators into generators for charging batteries. The full shop manuals are in Engines-Motors\ (Small-Engines, Chainsaws-and-Saws, Electric-Motors, Motors-as-Generators). Creek hydro and solar are in Off-Grid-Power\; electricity basics are in the Navy NEETS modules there. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - Never run an engine or generator indoors, in a garage, shed or crawlspace — carbon monoxide kills in minutes, even with doors open. - Never refuel a hot or running engine. Keep the can touching the tank while pouring (stops static sparks). - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet ("backfeeding") — use a transfer switch or interlock. It can kill someone working on the lines. - Capacitors bite. Motor capacitors (and microwave ovens) can hold a deadly charge after unplugging. Discharge across the terminals with an insulated screwdriver or a resistor before touching. - Pull the spark plug wire before working on a mower blade, saw chain or anything the engine turns.

⛽ Small gas engines: why it won't start Every engine needs three things: compression, spark and fuel. Find which one is missing. (MAVCC Small Engine Repair) 1. Fuel: pull the plug, cover the hole with a finger and pull the starter 2–3 times. A wet finger means fuel is arriving. If dry, check: fuel in the tank, shutoff valve open, cap vent not blocked, carburetor bowl (drain it — water or gum?), fuel filter and line. 2. Spark: put a spare plug on the plug wire, rest it against the metal head and crank. A bright blue spark is good. Yellow, weak or none = clean or replace the plug, check the kill-switch wire, then the coil/magneto. 3. Compression: spin the flywheel backward against compression — a sharp rebound is good. Weak = loose plug or head, stuck valve, worn rings. Old fuel is the #1 problem. Gas goes stale in about 60 days without stabilizer (sooner with ethanol). For longer storage, drain the tank and run the carburetor dry, or add stabilizer and run it a few minutes so it reaches the carburetor. Keep cans sealed — water in ethanol gas separates and ruins engines. (Oklahoma Extension BAE-1746) Cleaning a carburetor (AAVIM Small Engines Vol 2): - Take a photo before you take it apart. Soak metal parts several hours in carb cleaner, then blow out every passage with

a carburetor (AAVIM Small Engines Vol 2): - Take a photo before you take it apart. Soak metal parts several hours in carb cleaner, then blow out every passage with air. - Plastic or nylon parts no more than 30 minutes; never soak cork or coated floats. - Don't poke jets with wire — it enlarges them. Use a bristle, fishing line or air. - Always fit new gaskets. Float too high = floods; too low = starves. Two-stroke fuel (chainsaws, trimmers): mix oil at the ratio printed on the engine or in its manual. Never run straight gas — it seizes the engine in minutes. Rule of thumb: most modern saws are 50:1 (about 2.6 oz of 2-stroke oil per gallon); older gear is often 16:1–32:1. Don't mix mineral and synthetic 2-stroke oils. Routine care: check oil every use (4-strokes), clean the air filter often (a choked filter makes an engine run rich and weak), keep cooling fins clear, replace the plug yearly.

🪚 Chainsaws, crosscut saws and axes - A sharp chain throws chips; a dull one makes dust — and dust clogs the filter and raises kickback risk. (USFS Chain Saw and Crosscut Saw Training Course) - Filing: use the file size for your chain, with a guide. Hold the file level with about one-fifth of it above the cutter's top plate, guide mark parallel to the chain. File from the inside of each cutter outward, all of one side, then turn the saw around. Keep all cutters the same length. - Depth gauges (the little humps in front of each cutter): check with a gauge tool every few sharpenings, file down only to the tool, and round off the front. - Running out of fuel isn't the end of cutting. A sharp crosscut saw and ax still fell and buck trees. Raker depth for a crosscut: 0.008 in for hard, dry wood up to 0.030 in for soft, springy wood; start at about 0.012 in. (USFS Crosscut Saw Manual, Saws That Sing, An Ax to Grind)

🔋 Generators - Maintenance: oil change every 50–100 hours (sooner when new), clean air filter, fresh or stabilized fuel, run it under load for 20–30 minutes once a month. - Load: add up the running watts of what you'll plug in, plus the start surge of motors (fridges, pumps, power tools can need 2–3× their running watts for a second). Keep steady load under about 80% of the generator's rating. - Grounding: follow the generator's own manual. (The Army 3 kW set procedure is a ground rod at least 8 ft deep with No. 6 copper wire — TM 5-6115-271-14.) - No output but the engine runs? Check the breaker on the generator, then the brushes and voltage regulator (most small generators). A generator that sat unused can lose its residual magnetism — see "flashing the field" below.

⚙️ Electric motors: testing and repair Single-phase motor hums but won't start (pumps, compressors, shop tools): suspect the start capacitor or the centrifugal start switch, which should click open at about ¾ speed. Discharge the capacitor, check it (a bulged or leaking one is dead; a meter with a capacitance setting tells for sure), and replace with the same microfarads and same or higher voltage. (TM 5-683; Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use) Basic winding checks with a meter (Navy Electrician's Mate): - Windings must have no opens (infinite ohms through a winding), no shorts (much lower reading than its twin), and no grounds (any reading from a winding to the frame). - The three windings of a 3-phase motor should read nearly the same resistance. - Insulation test (megger): right after shutdown while warm and dry, with capacitors disconnected. At least 0.5 megohm for motors 250 V and under, 1 megohm up to 1000 V. (TM 5-683) - Armatures (brushed motors): test bar-to-bar on the commutator with a low-ohm meter; a "growler" finds shorted coils (a hacksaw blade buzzes over the bad coil). Bearings: a rumbling or hot bearing is the most common motor failure. Replace with the same number stamped on it. Fit new bearings by heating them to about 200 °F (oil bath or oven, not a flame). Never wash sealed bearings in solvent. Brushes and commutators

number stamped on it. Fit new bearings by heating them to about 200 °F (oil bath or oven, not a flame). Never wash sealed bearings in solvent. Brushes and commutators (drills, saws, mixers, car starters, DC motors): replace brushes before they're shorter than about ¼ in. Seat new brushes by pulling fine sandpaper (grit toward the brush) under them around the commutator, then blow out the carbon dust. A blackened, grooved commutator can be cleaned with a commutator stone or fine sandpaper, or turned lightly on a lathe (no more than 0.010 in per cut). Rewinding a burned motor (Braymer & Roe Rewinding Small Motors; DOE Repair Specifications): - Before stripping, record everything: turns per coil, wire size, coil span (slots), how coils connect, and lead markings. Photograph each step. - Strip old windings at no more than about 680 °F (360 °C) or the iron core is damaged. - Rewind with the same total copper area per turn and same turns (two thinner wires in parallel can replace one thick one). Varnish and bake below about 195 °F to dry. - Small burned motors are often easier to replace from salvage than to rewind — keep a stock.

🔁 Motors as generators What works best, easiest first: 1. Permanent-magnet DC motors (treadmill motors, wheelchair, scooter, some cordless tool motors): spin them and they make DC directly. Output voltage rises with speed, so choose one that makes at least 14–15 V at the speed you can actually turn it to charge a 12 V battery. Add a blocking diode so the battery can't run it as a motor. (Rule of thumb) 2. Car alternators: built-in rectifier and regulator, but they need about 1,500+ rpm (step-up pulleys or belts for wind, water or pedals) and a battery connected to power their field — they are not self-starting. The field draws about 3 A, which wastes a lot at low power. (ED021119 Alternator and Regulator Servicing) 3. Induction motors (ordinary AC motors) as generators: drive it faster than its synchronous speed by about as much as its rated slip — e.g. a motor rated 1725 rpm (1800 synchronous) is driven at about 1875 rpm. On its own (not tied to the grid) it needs capacitors across the windings to excite it. (DOE Microhydropower Handbook Vol 2, in Off-Grid-Power\Micro-Hydro) - Rule of thumb: start with run capacitors whose current at rated voltage roughly matches the motor's no-load current, then trim until voltage and frequency are right. Use AC motor-run (film) capacitors, never electrolytic start capacitors. - Expect about 70–80% of the motor's

roughly matches the motor's no-load current, then trim until voltage and frequency are right. Use AC motor-run (film) capacitors, never electrolytic start capacitors. - Expect about 70–80% of the motor's rating as output. Needs a ballast (dump) load or controller so voltage doesn't swing as loads switch. Aging capacitors make frequency creep up; a capacitor running hotter than the others is failing. (Practical Action Micro-Hydro O&M) 4. Build a permanent-magnet alternator from magnets and magnet wire for a wind turbine or slow water wheel — full plans in Hugh Piggott's Axial Flux Alternator and PMG Construction Manual. Rules for any homemade generator: - Never let a wind or water generator run with no load — it overspeeds and can destroy itself. Use a diversion (dump-load) charge controller, not a solar controller (solar controllers disconnect the source). (DFID-ITDG Small Wind Systems) - Flashing the field: if a generator or self-excited induction generator won't build up voltage, touch a 12 V battery briefly across one field or winding to restore residual magnetism, then try again. (Rule of thumb) - Old method: the 1939 North Dakota circular shows turning a car generator into a 6-volt wind charger, and the DOE Wind Power for Farms handbook covers matching any generator to a rotor.Measurements and settings in old manuals are fine for methods; for your specific engine, motor or generator, its own nameplate and manual

Farms handbook covers matching any generator to a rotor.Measurements and settings in old manuals are fine for methods; for your specific engine, motor or generator, its own nameplate and manual come first.

💊 Using found or expired medicines 1. Identify it. US pills must carry an imprint code. Open Pill-Identifier\PILL-IDENTIFIER.html, type the code, then check that the color, shape and size also match — the same code can be two different drugs (e.g. "I2" is ibuprofen 200 mg or amitriptyline 25 mg depending on size; "N 4" is nitroglycerin or a diet pill). No code at all = a supplement, a foreign or compounded product, or an illegal pill. 2. Never trust street pills. Pills that didn't come from a pharmacy can be counterfeits pressed with fentanyl — fake blue "M30" oxycodone, Xanax and Adderall are common, and many contain a deadly dose. 3. Look it up before giving it. In the WHO Model Formulary or MSF Essential Drugs (Medicines\), read what it treats, the dose, who must not take it, and interactions. For children, use the WHO Formulary for Children — children's doses go by weight. 4. Expired medicines. Most tablets and capsules kept sealed, cool and dry lose potency slowly — military testing extended most stockpiled lots by years, and some drugs kept 90% strength decades past their date. But: - Don't rely on expired or badly stored: insulin (lasts only ~28 days unrefrigerated; never use if it froze), nitroglycerin tablets (lose strength once opened — keep in the original glass bottle), epinephrine pens (weaker when expired — but an

only ~28 days unrefrigerated; never use if it froze), nitroglycerin tablets (lose strength once opened — keep in the original glass bottle), epinephrine pens (weaker when expired — but an expired pen with clear liquid is better than none in anaphylaxis), and mixed liquid antibiotics (amoxicillin suspension: 14 days in the fridge). - Throw out anything discolored, crumbling, sticky or smelling odd — especially tetracycline-family antibiotics, which can damage the kidneys when degraded. - Store medicines cool and dry (not the bathroom, kitchen or a car), in their original containers, out of children's reach. 5. The biggest dangers - Allergy — face or throat swelling, trouble breathing or widespread hives after a medicine is anaphylaxis: give epinephrine if you have it. - Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — no more than 4,000 mg a day for adults, counting every product; it's hidden in Norco, Vicodin, Percocet and many cold medicines. Too much causes liver failure. - Opioids — a dose that's normal for someone used to them can stop the breathing of someone who isn't, or of a child. Never combine with benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium, Klonopin), alcohol or other sedatives. Naloxone (Narcan) reverses opioid overdose — keep some. - Children — no cough/cold medicines under age 2, no aspirin for children or teens. - Interactions — check the formulary when someone already takes blood thinners, heart medicines or antidepressants. - Poisoning: Oregon Poison

medicines under age 2, no aspirin for children or teens. - Interactions — check the formulary when someone already takes blood thinners, heart medicines or antidepressants. - Poisoning: Oregon Poison Center 1-800-222-1222 (24/7, while phones work). Stock up now: ask your doctor about extra supplies of the medicines your household depends on, and keep an emergency kit (wound care, pain/fever medicine, antihistamines, oral rehydration salts, naloxone).
Ask an AI about the PDFs On a laptop, use the Library Assistant (searches everything, answers with sources), or GPT4All (AI-Offline\DocReader-GPT4All\) with the medical folders added as a collection.

⚠️ Important This is reference information, not a substitute for a doctor. Books and offline AIs can be wrong or out of date. Get professional help whenever it's possible; use this when it isn't, and double-check anything critical against more than one source. Hesperian and MSF books are free for personal use; ask the publishers before giving copies to others.

Ham (Amateur), CB, Shortwave, GMRS/FRS & MURS — how they work and how to use them This guide explains, in plain language, how to communicate by radio when the internet and phones are down. It covers what each type of radio is, what it can do, which frequencies/channels matter in an emergency, and the basic procedures for calling for help. Legal note (normal times): Transmitting on ham (amateur) frequencies requires a license (easy to get — see below). GMRS requires a cheap license (no test). CB, FRS, MURS need no license. Shortwave listening needs no license (you're only receiving). In a genuine life-threatening emergency, FCC rules (47 CFR §97.405) let anyone use any means of radio to call for help. Listening is always legal. Learn and practice before you need it.

1. The quick version — what to grab and what to know | Need | Best tool | License | Range (typical) | | Talk to family nearby (same property / neighborhood) | FRS / GMRS walkie-talkie | FRS none; GMRS cheap | 0.5–2 mi (up to 5+ with GMRS + height) | | Talk across town / coordinate a group | GMRS (with repeater) or Ham VHF/UHF | GMRS cheap; Ham test | 5–50 mi via repeater | | Talk regionally / long distance / into other states | Ham HF | Ham (General class) | 100s–1000s mi | | Hear news & official broadcasts from anywhere | Shortwave receiver | none (listening) | Worldwide | | Road / vehicle convoy, truckers | CB | none | 1–15 mi | Three things everyone should know: 1. Monitor, don't just transmit. A cheap receiver tells you what's happening. 2. Higher antenna = more range. Antenna height matters more than watts. 3. Have a plan: agree on a channel/frequency and check-in times with your group in advance (write them down — see the card at the end).

2. How radio actually works (the 60-second version) - A radio turns your voice into radio waves at a certain frequency (measured in kilohertz kHz or megahertz MHz). Another radio tuned to the same frequency turns the wave back into sound. - Both radios must be on the same frequency/channel AND the same mode (e.g. FM, AM, SSB) to hear each other. - Only one person talks at a time. You press PTT (push-to-talk) to transmit, release it to listen. You cannot hear others while you hold PTT. - Frequency bands behave very differently: - VHF/UHF (high frequency numbers, ~30 MHz–3 GHz): travel in roughly straight "line of sight." Great locally, blocked by hills/buildings. Used by FRS, GMRS, MURS, and ham 2m/70cm. Extended by repeaters (see below). - HF / shortwave (low numbers, ~3–30 MHz): can bounce off the ionosphere and travel hundreds or thousands of miles ("skip"). Used by ham HF, CB (27 MHz), and shortwave broadcasters. Range changes with time of day and the sun.

3. CB Radio (Citizens Band) — no license, simple, vehicle-friendly - What it is: 40 channels around 27 MHz (in the HF band). No license needed. Cheap, everywhere, popular with truckers and off-roaders. - Range: usually 1–15 miles (more in flat/open terrain; occasionally hundreds of miles when "skip" conditions bounce signals off the ionosphere). - Power limit: 4 watts AM / 12 watts SSB (SSB radios reach farther). - Key channels: - Channel 9 — traditional emergency / help channel. - Channel 19 — highway / trucker channel (road conditions, traffic, convoys). - Channel 1–40 — general use; pick an unused one for your group. - Modes: Most CB is AM. Higher-end radios add SSB (USB/LSB) for more range — but both radios must use the same mode. - Good for: vehicle-to-vehicle, convoys, short local coordination with zero setup.
4. FRS / GMRS / MURS — the walkie-talkie families These are the little handheld radios ("walkie-talkies"). Great for family/group.

FRS (Family Radio Service) — no license - The blister-pack walkie-talkies. 22 channels in UHF (462/467 MHz). - Low power (0.5–2 W), fixed antenna. Range ~0.5–2 miles. - No license, no setup. Good for keeping a family/group in touch on foot.

GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) — cheap license, no test - Shares channels with FRS but allows higher power (up to 50 W), detachable antennas, and repeaters — so range can reach 5–50+ miles via a repeater. - One GMRS license (~$35, no exam) covers your entire family for 10 years. - Best all-round family emergency radio: cheap, legal, powerful, easy.
MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service) — no license - 5 channels in VHF (151/154 MHz), up to 2 W. No license. - VHF often works better outdoors/rural than FRS/GMRS UHF. Good for property/farm.

5. Ham (Amateur) Radio — the serious emergency option Ham radio is the backbone of emergency communications. When everything else fails, hams relay health-and-welfare traffic, weather, and coordination across towns, states, and continents.

Licensing (USA) — easier than you think Three license levels, each a multiple-choice test (questions are public — you can study the exact pool): 1. Technician — entry level. Grants VHF/UHF (local, repeaters) plus some HF. Enough for local/regional emergency comms. ~1 evening of study. 2. General — adds most HF privileges → long-distance / cross-country. 3. Amateur Extra — full privileges. Get at least a Technician license now while it's easy, and ideally General so you can use HF for long distance. In a true emergency you may legally transmit without a license to save life/property — but you'll be far more effective if you've practiced.

The main ham bands and what they do - 2 meters (144–148 MHz, VHF) and 70 cm (420–450 MHz, UHF): local simplex + repeaters. Your everyday "talk around town" bands. - HF bands (e.g. 80m, 40m, 20m): long distance. - 40m (7 MHz): reliable regional (100s of miles), day and night — great for a state/region emergency net. - 20m (14 MHz): long-distance (cross-country / international) in daytime. - 80m (3.5 MHz): regional at night.

Repeaters — how hams get range from a handheld A repeater is a radio on a tower/hilltop that receives your weak signal and re-transmits it with a big antenna and power, massively extending range. To use one you set your radio to the repeater's output frequency, an offset (so it transmits on the input), and sometimes a CTCSS "tone." Local repeater lists (and emergency nets) are worth printing out for your area.
Simplex (radio-to-radio, no repeater) If repeaters are down, you talk simplex — directly, radio to radio, line of sight. The national 2m simplex calling frequency is 146.520 MHz.

Ham digital & data (advanced, FYI) Hams can also send text/email/images with no internet via Winlink (email over radio), FT8 (weak-signal), and APRS (position/text). Useful but needs more gear and practice.

6. Shortwave (SWL) — hearing the outside world - What it is: Using a shortwave receiver to listen to broadcasts on the HF bands (roughly 1.8–30 MHz). No license needed to listen. - Why it matters: When local media and internet are down, shortwave lets you hear international news, government/emergency broadcasts, and ham traffic from far away — because HF signals bounce worldwide. - What to listen for: - International broadcasters (news from outside the affected area). - NOAA Weather Radio (VHF 162.400–162.550 MHz) — continuous US weather & emergency alerts. Every emergency kit should have a NOAA weather radio. - Ham bands (40m/20m) — to hear emergency nets and relays. - AM/FM broadcast and Emergency Alert System (EAS) on a normal radio. - Modes: Broadcasts are usually AM; ham/utility voice is often SSB (USB/LSB). A radio with SSB hears far more. - Tip: A simple long wire antenna dramatically improves shortwave reception.

7. Antennas, power & range (the practical stuff) - Antenna height beats power. Getting the antenna up high (roof, tree, mast) adds more range than buying a bigger amplifier. - Use the right antenna for the band. A proper resonant antenna (correct length for the frequency) works far better than a random wire. - Line of sight (VHF/UHF): range ≈ limited by the horizon and obstructions. Height = range. Repeaters overcome this. - HF skip: range changes with the time of day and solar conditions. Lower bands (80m) are better at night; higher bands (20m) are better in daytime. - Power: keep radios charged. Stock spare batteries, a 12V battery, a solar panel, and car-charging cables. A radio with a dead battery is a paperweight. - Grounding & safety: never put an antenna where it can touch power lines; ground equipment to reduce static/lightning risk.

8. How to call for help (procedure) 1. Listen first. Make sure you're not interrupting other emergency traffic. 2. Use the emergency call: - Voice distress: say "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY" (life-threatening) or "PAN-PAN" (urgent but not immediately life-threatening), then your info. - On CB, call on Channel 9. On ham, break into the local emergency net or call on a repeater / 146.520 simplex. 3. Give the essentials — slowly, clearly, repeat: - Who you are (name / call sign). - Where you are (address, cross-streets, GPS coords, landmarks). - What the emergency is (injury, fire, trapped, etc.). - What you need (medical, rescue, relay a message). 4. Spell hard words with the phonetic alphabet (below). 5. Stay on, don't wander off frequency. Keep the radio on so responders can call back. Repeat your message at intervals if no answer.

NATO phonetic alphabet Alpha Bravo Charlie Delta Echo Foxtrot Golf Hotel India Juliet Kilo Lima Mike November Oscar Papa Quebec Romeo Sierra Tango Uniform Victor Whiskey X-ray Yankee Zulu. Numbers: say digits individually ("one-two-zero").

Common "pro-words" - "Over" = I'm done talking, your turn. - "Out" = conversation finished (don't say "over and out"). - "Roger" / "Copy" = I received and understand. - "Say again" = repeat (don't say "repeat"). - "Affirmative / Negative" = yes / no. - "Break" = pause / someone with emergency traffic wants in.

9. A sensible emergency radio kit (shopping / checklist) - [ ] NOAA weather radio (hand-crank/solar + battery) — alerts & forecasts. - [ ] Shortwave receiver with SSB — hear news & ham traffic worldwide (RX only). - [ ] A pair+ of GMRS radios (and a GMRS license) — family/group, best bang for buck. FRS works with no license at shorter range. - [ ] A dual-band (2m/70cm) ham handheld (HT) — cheap; huge capability with a Technician license. Add a better antenna. - [ ] (Advanced) An HF ham radio + General license — true long distance. - [ ] CB if you travel by vehicle/convoy. - [ ] Power: spare batteries, 12V battery, solar panel, car charger. - [ ] Better antennas + coax; a roll of wire for an HF/long-wire antenna. - [ ] Printed frequency card (below), local repeater list, notebook & pencil.

10. Print-and-keep frequency card Fill in your group's agreed channels and local repeaters, then print this page. ===================== EMERGENCY RADIO CARD ===================== Our group PRIMARY channel : _______________ Mode: _______ Our group BACKUP channel : _______________ Mode: _______ Check-in times (daily) : _______ _______ _______ CB emergency / help ....... Channel 9 CB highway / travel ....... Channel 19 Ham 2m simplex calling .... 146.520 MHz (FM) NOAA Weather Radio ........ 162.400 / 162.425 / 162.450 / 162.475 / 162.500 / 162.525 / 162.550 MHz FRS/GMRS family channel ... _______ (GMRS license #: __________) Local repeaters (output / offset / tone): 1) ________ MHz / ____ / tone ______ (____________) 2) ________ MHz / ____ / tone ______ (____________) 3) ________ MHz / ____ / tone ______ (____________) Distress voice: "MAYDAY x3" (life threat) or "PAN-PAN x3" (urgent) Say: WHO you are - WHERE you are - WHAT's wrong - WHAT you need ==================================================================

11. Where to learn more offline (already in this kit) - Appropedia and iFixit archives (in E:\Manuals\, via the Kiwix reader) include antenna, electronics and repair articles. - WikiMed / Wikipedia-medicine (E:\Medical\) for treating injuries while you wait for help. - Study the ham license question pools (download them now while you have internet; the exact questions and answers are public) so you can get licensed quickly. Practice now: tune around, learn your radios' menus, program the channels above, and do a test check-in with your group. Skills and muscle memory matter more than gear.

FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL PATTERN FOR SURVIVAL Develop a survival pattern that lets you beat the enemies of survival. This survival pattern must include food, water, shelter, fire, first aid, and signals placed in order of importance. For example, in a cold environment, you would need a fire to get warm; a shelter to protect you from the cold, wind, and rain or snow; traps or snares to get food; a means to signal friendly aircraft; and first aid to maintain health. If injured, first aid has top priority no matter what climate you are in. Change your survival pattern to meet your immediate physical needs as the environment changes. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 2 - PSYCHOLOGY OF SURVIVAL It takes much more than the knowledge and skills to build shelters, get food, make fires, and travel without the aid of standard navigational devices to live successfully through a survival situation. Some people with little or no survival training have managed to survive life-threatening circumstances. Some people with survival training have not used their skills and died. A key ingredient in any survival situation is the mental attitude of the individual(s) involved. Having survival skills is important; having the will to survive is essential. Without a desk to survive, acquired skills serve little purpose and invaluable knowledge goes to waste. There is a psychology to survival. The soldier in a survival environment faces many stresses that ultimately impact on his mind. These stresses can produce thoughts and emotions that, if poorly understood, can transform a confident, well-trained soldier into an indecisive, ineffective individual with questionable ability to survive. Thus, every soldier must be aware of and be able to recognize those stresses commonly associated with survival. Additionally, it is imperative that soldiers be aware of their reactions to the wide variety of stresses associated with survival. This

FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL Any event can lead to stress and, as everyone has experienced, events don't always come one at a time. Often, stressful events occur simultaneously. These events are not stress, but they produce it and are called "stressors." Stressors are the obvious cause while stress is the response. Once the body recognizes the presence of a stressor, it then begins to act to protect itself. In response to a stressor, the body prepares either to "fight or flee." This preparation involves an internal SOS sent throughout the body. As the body responds to this SOS, several actions take place. The body releases stored fuels (sugar and fats) to provide quick energy; breathing rate increases to supply more oxygen to the blood; muscle tension increases to prepare for action; blood clotting mechanisms are activated to reduce bleeding from cuts; senses become more acute (hearing becomes more sensitive, eyes become big, smell becomes sharper) so that you are more aware of your surrounding and heart rate and blood pressure rise to provide more blood to the muscles. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 3 - SURVIVAL PLANNING AND SURVIVAL KITS Survival planning is nothing more than realizing something could happen that would put you in a survival situation and, with that in mind, taking steps to increase your chances of survival. Thus, survival planning means preparation. Preparation means having survival items and knowing how to use them People who live in snow regions prepare their vehicles for poor road conditions. They put snow tires on their vehicles, add extra weight in the back for traction, and they carry a shovel, salt, and a blanket. Another example of preparation is finding the emergency exits on an aircraft when you board it for a flight. Preparation could also mean knowing your intended route of travel and familiarizing yourself with the area. Finally, emergency planning is essential. A cut artery issues bright red blood from the wound in distinct spurts or pulses that correspond to the rhythm of the heartbeat. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL Dislocations Dislocations are the separations of bone joints causing the bones to go out of proper alignment. These misalignments can be extremely painful and can cause an impairment of nerve or circulatory function below the area affected. You must place these joints back into alignment as quickly as possible. Signs and symptoms of dislocations are joint pain, tenderness, swelling, discoloration, limited range of motion, and deformity of the joint. You treat dislocations by reduction, immobilization, and rehabilitation. Reduction or "setting" is placing the bones back into their proper alignment. The basic types of root structures (Figure 9-4) are the bulb, clove, taproot, tuber, rhizome, corm, and crown. Bulbs are familiar to us as onions and, when sliced in half, will show concentric rings. Cloves are those bulblike structures that remind us of garlic and will separate into small pieces when broken apart. This characteristic separates wild onions from wild garlic. They are mostly nocturnal in habit. You can find desert scorpions from below sea level in Death Valley to elevations as high as 3,600 meters in the Andes. Typically brown or black in moist areas, they may be yellow or light green in the desert. Their average size is about 2.5 centimeters. However, there are 20-centimeter giants in the jungles of Central America, New Guinea, and southern Africa. Fatalities from scorpion stings are rare, but they can occur in children, the elderly, and ill persons. Scorpions resemble small lobsters with raised, jointed tails bearing a stinger in the tip. Nature mimics the scorpions with whip scorpions or vinegar-roons. These are harmless and have a tail like a wire or whip, rather than the jointed tail and stinger of true scorpions. They are small, agile fliers that land on their sleeping victims, mostly cows and horses, to lap a blood meal after biting their victim. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL POISONOUS SNAKES There are no infallible rules for expedient identification of poisonous snakes in the field, because the guidelines all require close observation or manipulation of the snake's body. The best strategy is to leave all snakes alone. Where snakes are plentiful and poisonous species are present, the risk of their bites negates their food value. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 12 - FIELD-EXPEDIENT WEAPONS, TOOLS, AND EQUIPMENT As a soldier you know the importance of proper care and use of your weapons, tools, and equipment. This is especially true of your knife. You must always keep it sharp and ready to use. A knife is your most valuable tool in a survival situation. Imagine being in a survival situation without any weapons, tools, or equipment except your knife. It could happen! You might even be without a knife. You would probably feel helpless, but with the proper knowledge and skills, you can easily improvise needed items. In survival situations, you may have to fashion any number and type of fieldexpedient tools and equipment to survive. Examples of tools and equipment that could make your life much easier are ropes, rucksacks, clothes, nets, and so on. Weapons serve a dual purpose. You use them to obtain and prepare food and to provide self-defense. A weapon can also give you a feeling of security and provide you with the ability to hunt on the move. The weight may be a natural weight, such as a knot on the wood, or something added, such as a stone lashed to the club. To make a weighted club, first find a stone that has a shape that will allow you to lash it securely to the club. A stone with a slight hourglass shape works well. If you cannot find a suitably shaped stone, you must fashion a groove or channel into the stone by a technique known as pecking. By repeatedly rapping the club stone with a smaller hard stone, you can get the desired shape. Next, find a piece of wood that is the right length for you. A straight-grained hardwood is best. The length of the wood should feel comfortable in relation to the weight of the stone. Finally, lash the stone to the handle. Cover and concealment may be very limited; therefore, the threat of exposure to the enemy remains constant. The sun always rises in the east and sets in the west, but not exactly due east or due west. There is also some seasonal variation. Preface As a soldier, you can be sent to any area of the world. It may be in a temperate, tropical, arctic, or subarctic region. You expect to have all your personal equipment and your unit members with you wherever you go. However, there is no guarantee it will be so. You could find yourself alone in a remote area— possibly enemy territory—with little or no personal gear. This manual provides information and describes basic techniques that will enable you to survive and return alive should you find yourself in such a situation. If you are a trainer, use this information as a base on which to build survival training. You know the areas to which your unit is likely to deploy, the means by which it will travel, and the territory through which it will travel. Read what this manual says about survival in those particular areas and find out all you can about those areas. Read other books on survival. Develop a survival-training program that will enable your unit members to meet any survival situation they may face. It can make the difference between life and death. Chapter 1 Introduction This manual is based entirely on the keyword SURVIVAL. The letters in this word can help guide your actions in any survival situation. Learn what each letter represents and practice applying these guidelines when conducting survival training. Remember the word SURVIVAL. SURVIVAL ACTIONS 1-1. The following paragraphs expand on the meaning of each letter of the word survival. Study and remember what each letter signifies because some day you may have to make the word work for you. S—SIZE UP THE SITUATION 1-2. If you are in a combat situation, find a place where you can conceal yourself from the enemy. Remember, security takes priority. Use your senses of hearing, smell, and sight to get a feel for the battlespace. Determine if the enemy is attacking, defending, or withdrawing. You will have to consider what is developing on the battlespace when you make your survival plan. Surroundings 1-3. Determine the pattern of the area. Get a feel for what is going on around you. Every environment, whether forest, jungle, or desert, has a rhythm or pattern. This tempo includes animal and bird noises and movements and insect sounds. It may also include enemy traffic and civilian movements.

This basic principle is one that you must always follow. If there are other persons with you, make sure they also know their location. The greatest enemies in a combat survival and evasion situation are fear and panic. If uncontrolled, they can destroy your ability to make an intelligent decision. They may cause you to react to your feelings and imagination rather than to your situation. These emotions can drain your energy and thereby cause other negative emotions. Previous survival and evasion training and self-confidence will enable you to vanquish fear and panic. I—IMPROVISE 1-11. In the United States (U.S.), we have items available for all our needs. This inexperience in “making do” can be an enemy in a survival situation. Learn to improvise. Take a tool designed for a specific purpose and see how many other uses you can make of it. 1-12. No matter how complete a survival kit you have with you, it will run out or wear out after a while. Your imagination must take over when your kit wears out. V—VALUE LIVING 1-13. All of us were born kicking and fighting to live, but we have become used to the soft life. We have become creatures of comfort. We dislike inconveniences and discomforts. What happens when we are faced with a survival situation with its stresses, inconveniences, and discomforts? This is when the will to live— placing a high value on living—is vital. The experience and knowledge you have gained through life and your Army training will have a bearing on your will to live. Stubbornness, a refusal to give in to problems and obstacles that face you, will give you the mental and physical strength to endure. 1-3

FM 3-05.70 A—ACT LIKE THE NATIVES 1-14. The natives and animals of a region have adapted to their environment. To get a feel of the area, watch how the people go about their daily routine. When and what do they eat? When, where, and how do they get their food? When and where do they go for water? What time do they usually go to bed and get up? These actions are important to you when you are trying to avoid capture. 1-15. Animal life in the area can also give you clues on how to survive. Animals also require food, water, and shelter. By watching them, you can find sources of water and food. WARNING Animals cannot serve as an absolute guide to what you can eat and drink. Many animals eat plants that are toxic to humans. 1-16. Keep in mind that the reaction of animals can reveal your presence to the enemy. 1-17. If in a friendly area, one way you can gain rapport with the natives is to show interest in their tools and how they get food and water. By studying the people, you learn to respect them, you often make valuable friends, and, most

L—LIVE BY YOUR WITS, BUT FOR NOW, LEARN BASIC SKILLS 1-18. Without training in basic skills for surviving and evading on the battlespace, your chances of living through a combat survival and evasion situation are slight. 1-19. Learn these basic skills now—not when you are headed for or are in the battle. How you decide to equip yourself before deployment will affect whether or not you survive. You need to know about the environment to which you are going, and you must practice basic skills geared to that environment. For instance, if you are going to a desert, you need to know how to get water. 1-4

FM 3-05.70 1-20. Practice basic survival skills during all training programs and exercises. Survival training reduces fear of the unknown and gives you self-confidence. It teaches you to live by your wits. PATTERN FOR SURVIVAL 1-21. Develop a survival pattern that lets you beat the enemies of survival. This survival pattern must include food, water, shelter, fire, first aid, and signals placed in order of importance. For example, in a cold environment, you would need a fire to get warm; a shelter to protect you from the cold, wind, and rain or snow; traps or snares to get food; a means to signal friendly aircraft; and first aid to maintain health. If you are injured, first aid has top priority no matter what climate you are in. 1-22. Change your survival pattern to meet your immediate physical needs as the environment changes. Chapter 2 Psychology of Survival It takes much more than the knowledge and skills to build shelters, get food, make fires, and travel without the aid of standard navigational devices to live successfully through a survival situation. Some people with little or no survival training have managed to survive lifethreatening circumstances. Some people with survival training have not used their skills and died. A key ingredient in any survival situation is the mental attitude of the individual involved. Having survival skills is important; having the will to survive is essential. Without a desire to survive, acquired skills serve little purpose and invaluable knowledge goes to waste. There is a psychology to survival. You will face many stressors in a survival environment that ultimately will affect your mind. These stressors can produce thoughts and emotions that, if poorly understood, can transform a confident, well-trained person into an indecisive, ineffective individual with questionable ability to survive. Thus, you must be aware of and be able to recognize those stressors commonly associated with survival. It is also imperative that you be aware of your reactions to the wide variety of stressors associated with survival. This chapter identifies and explains the nature of stress,

and be able to recognize those stressors commonly associated with survival. It is also imperative that you be aware of your reactions to the wide variety of stressors associated with survival. This chapter identifies and explains the nature of stress, the stressors of survival, and those internal reactions that you will naturally experience when faced with the stressors of a real-world survival situation. The knowledge you gain from this chapter and the remainder of this manual, will prepare you to come through the toughest times alive. 2-1

FM 3-05.70 A LOOK AT STRESS 2-1. Before we can understand our psychological reactions in a survival setting, it is helpful to first know a little bit about stress and its effects. Stress is not a disease that you cure and eliminate. Instead, it is a condition we all experience. Stress can be described as our reaction to pressure. It is the name given to the experience we have as we physically, mentally, emotionally, and spiritually respond to life’s tensions. NEED FOR STRESS 2-2. We need stress because it has many positive benefits. Stress provides us with challenges; it gives us chances to learn about our values and strengths. Stress can show our ability to handle pressure without breaking. It tests our adaptability and flexibility, and can stimulate us to do our best. Because we usually do not consider unimportant events stressful, stress can also be an excellent indicator of the significance we attach to an event—in other words, it highlights what is important to us. 2-3. We need to have some stress in our lives, but too much of anything can be bad. The goal is to have stress, but not an excess of it. Too much stress can

highlights what is important to us. 2-3. We need to have some stress in our lives, but too much of anything can be bad. The goal is to have stress, but not an excess of it. Too much stress can take its toll on people and organizations. Too much stress leads to distress. Distress causes an uncomfortable tension that we try to escape or, preferably, avoid. Listed below are a few of the common signs of distress that you may encounter when faced with too much stress: • Difficulty making decisions. • Angry outbursts. • Forgetfulness. • Low energy level. • Constant worrying. • Propensity for mistakes. • Thoughts about death or suicide. • Trouble getting along with others. • Withdrawing from others. • Hiding from responsibilities. • Carelessness. 2-2

FM 3-05.70 2-4. As you can see, stress can be constructive or destructive. It can encourage or discourage, move us along or stop us dead in our tracks, and make life meaningful or seemingly meaningless. Stress can inspire you to operate successfully and perform at your maximum efficiency in a survival situation. It can also cause you to panic and forget all your training. Your key to survival is your ability to manage the inevitable stresses you will encounter. The person that survives is one who works with his stresses instead of letting his stresses work on him. SURVIVAL STRESSORS 2-5. Any event can lead to stress and, as everyone has experienced, events don’t always come one at a time. Often, stressful events occur simultaneously. These events are not stress, but they produce it and are called “stressors.” Stressors are the obvious cause while stress is the response. Once the body recognizes the presence of a stressor, it then begins to act to protect itself. 2-6. In response to a stressor, the body prepares either to “fight or flee.” This preparation involves an internal SOS sent throughout the body. As the body responds to this SOS, the following actions take

to act to protect itself. 2-6. In response to a stressor, the body prepares either to “fight or flee.” This preparation involves an internal SOS sent throughout the body. As the body responds to this SOS, the following actions take place: • The body releases stored fuels (sugar and fats) to provide quick energy. • Breathing rate increases to supply more oxygen to the blood. • Muscle tension increases to prepare for action. • Blood clotting mechanisms are activated to reduce bleeding from cuts. • Senses become more acute (hearing becomes more sensitive, pupils dilate, smell becomes sharper) so that you are more aware of your surroundings. • Heart rate and blood pressure rise to provide more blood to the muscles. This protective posture lets you cope with potential dangers. However, you cannot maintain this level of alertness indefinitely. 2-7. Stressors are not courteous; one stressor does not leave because another one arrives. Stressors add up. The cumulative 2-3

FM 3-05.70 effect of minor stressors can be a major distress if they all happen too close together. As the body’s resistance to stress wears down and the sources of stress continue (or increase), eventually a state of exhaustion arrives. At this point, the ability to resist stress or use it in a positive way gives out and signs of distress appear. Anticipating stressors and developing strategies to cope with them are two ingredients in the effective management of stress. Therefore, it is essential that you be aware of the types of stressors that you will encounter. The following paragraphs explain a few of these. Injury, Illness, or Death 2-8. Injury, illness, and death are real possibilities that you have to face. Perhaps nothing is more stressful than being alone in an unfamiliar environment where you could die from hostile action, an accident, or from eating something lethal. Illness and injury can also add to stress by limiting your ability to maneuver, get food and drink, find shelter, and defend yourself. Even if illness and injury don’t lead to death, they add to stress through the pain and discomfort they generate. It is only by controlling the stress associated with

to maneuver, get food and drink, find shelter, and defend yourself. Even if illness and injury don’t lead to death, they add to stress through the pain and discomfort they generate. It is only by controlling the stress associated with the vulnerability to injury, illness, and death that you can have the courage to take the risks associated with survival tasks. Uncertainty and Lack of Control 2-9. Some people have trouble operating in settings where everything is not clear-cut. The only guarantee in a survival situation is that nothing is guaranteed. It can be extremely stressful operating on limited information in a setting where you have limited control of your surroundings. This uncertainty and lack of control also add to the stress of being ill, injured, or killed. Environment 2-10. Even under the most ideal circumstances, nature is quite formidable. In survival, you will have to contend with the stressors of weather, terrain, and the variety of creatures inhabiting an area. Heat, cold, rain, winds, mountains, swamps, deserts, insects, dangerous reptiles, and other animals are just a few of the challenges that you will encounter while working to survive. Thus, getting and preserving food and water takes on increasing importance as the length of time in a survival setting increases. Foraging can also be a big source of stress since you are used to having your provisions issued. Fatigue 2-12. Forcing yourself to continue surviving is not easy as you grow more tired. Being in contact with others also provides a greater sense of security and a feeling someone is available to help if problems occur. A significant stressor in survival situations is that often you have to rely solely on your own resources. 2-14. The survival stressors mentioned in

a greater sense of security and a feeling someone is available to help if problems occur. A significant stressor in survival situations is that often you have to rely solely on your own resources. 2-14. The survival stressors mentioned in this section are by no means the only ones you may face. Remember, what is stressful to one person may not be stressful to another. Your experiences, training, personal outlook on life, physical and mental conditioning, and level of self-confidence contribute to what you will find stressful in a survival environment. The object is not to avoid stress, but rather to manage the stressors of survival and make them work for you. 2-15. We now have a general knowledge of stress and the stressors common to survival. FM 3-05.70 NATURAL REACTIONS 2-16. Man has been able to survive many shifts in his environment throughout the centuries. His ability to adapt physically and mentally to a changing world kept him alive while other species around him gradually died off. The same survival mechanisms that kept our forefathers alive can help keep you alive as well! However, the survival mechanisms that can help you can also work against you if you do not understand and anticipate their presence. 2-17. It is not surprising that the average person will have some psychological reactions in a survival situation. The following paragraphs explain some of the major internal reactions that you or anyone with you might experience with the previously stated survival stressors. FEAR 2-18. Fear is our emotional response to dangerous circumstances that we believe have the potential to cause death, injury, or illness. This harm is not just limited to physical damage; the threat to your emotional and mental well-being can generate fear as well. If you are trying to survive, fear can have a positive function if it encourages you to be cautious in situations where recklessness could result in injury. Unfortunately, fear can also immobilize you. It can

can generate fear as well. If you are trying to survive, fear can have a positive function if it encourages you to be cautious in situations where recklessness could result in injury. Unfortunately, fear can also immobilize you. It can cause you to become so frightened that you fail to perform activities essential for survival. Most people will have some degree of fear when placed in unfamiliar surroundings under adverse conditions. There is no shame in this! You must train yourself not to be overcome by your fears. Ideally, through realistic training, you can acquire the knowledge and skills needed to increase your confidence and thereby manage your fears. ANXIETY 2-19. Associated with fear is anxiety. Because it is natural for you to be afraid, it is also natural for you to experience anxiety. Anxiety can be an uneasy, apprehensive feeling you get when faced with dangerous situations (physical, mental, and emotional). When used in a healthy way, anxiety can urge you to act to end, or at least master, the dangers that threaten your 2-6

FM 3-05.70 existence. If you were never anxious, there would be little motivation to make changes in your life. In a survival setting you can reduce your anxiety by performing those tasks that will ensure you come through the ordeal alive. As you reduce your anxiety, you also bring under control the source of that anxiety— your fears. In this form, anxiety is good; however, anxiety can also have a devastating impact. Anxiety can overwhelm you to the point where you become easily confused and have difficulty thinking. Once this happens, it will become increasingly difficult for you to make good judgments and sound decisions. To survive, you must learn techniques to calm your anxieties and keep them in the range where they help, not hurt. ANGER AND FRUSTRATION 2-20. Frustration arises when you are continually thwarted in your attempts to reach a goal. The goal of survival is to stay alive until you can reach help or until help can reach you. To achieve this goal, you must complete some tasks with minimal resources. It is inevitable, in trying to do these tasks, that something will go wrong; that something will happen beyond your control; and that with your

can reach you. To achieve this goal, you must complete some tasks with minimal resources. It is inevitable, in trying to do these tasks, that something will go wrong; that something will happen beyond your control; and that with your life at stake, every mistake is magnified in terms of its importance. Thus, eventually, you will have to cope with frustration when a few of your plans run into trouble. One outgrowth of this frustration is anger. There are many events in a survival situation that can frustrate or anger you. Getting lost, damaged or forgotten equipment, the weather, inhospitable terrain, enemy patrols, and physical limitations are just a few sources of frustration and anger. Frustration and anger generate impulsive reactions, irrational behavior, poorly thought-out decisions, and, in some instances, an “I quit” attitude (people sometimes avoid doing something they can’t master). If you can harness and properly channel the emotional intensity associated with anger and frustration, you can productively act as you answer the challenges of survival. If you do not properly focus your angry feelings, you can waste much energy in activities that do little to further either your chances of survival or the chances of those around

act as you answer the challenges of survival. If you do not properly focus your angry feelings, you can waste much energy in activities that do little to further either your chances of survival or the chances of those around you. DEPRESSION 2-21. You would be a rare person indeed if you did not get sad, at least momentarily, when faced with the hardships of survival. As 2-7

FM 3-05.70 this sadness deepens, it becomes “depression.” Depression is closely linked with frustration and anger. Frustration will cause you to become increasingly angry as you fail to reach your goals. If the anger does not help you succeed, then the frustration level goes even higher. A destructive cycle between anger and frustration will continue until you become worn down— physically, emotionally, and mentally. When you reach this point, you start to give up, and your focus shifts from “What can I do” to “There is nothing I can do.” Depression is an expression of this hopeless, helpless feeling. There is nothing wrong with being sad as you temporarily think about your loved ones and remember what life is like back in “civilization” or “the world.” Such thoughts, in fact, can give you the desire to try harder and live one more day. On the other hand, if you allow yourself to sink into a depressed state, then it can sap all your energy and, more important, your will to survive. It is imperative that you resist succumbing to depression. LONELINESS AND BOREDOM 2-22. Man is a social animal. Human beings enjoy the company of others. Very few people want

sap all your energy and, more important, your will to survive. It is imperative that you resist succumbing to depression. LONELINESS AND BOREDOM 2-22. Man is a social animal. Human beings enjoy the company of others. Very few people want to be alone all the time! There is a distinct chance of isolation in a survival setting. Isolation is not bad. Loneliness and boredom can bring to the surface qualities you thought only others had. The extent of your imagination and creativity may surprise you. When required to do so, you may discover some hidden talents and abilities. Most of all, you may tap into a reservoir of inner strength and fortitude you never knew you had. Conversely, loneliness and boredom can be another source of depression. If you are surviving alone, or with others, you must find ways to keep your mind productively occupied. Additionally, you must develop a degree of selfsufficiency. You must have faith in your capability to “go it alone.” GUILT 2-23. The circumstances leading to your being in a survival setting are sometimes dramatic and tragic. It may be the result of an accident or military mission where there was a loss of life. Perhaps

to “go it alone.” GUILT 2-23. The circumstances leading to your being in a survival setting are sometimes dramatic and tragic. It may be the result of an accident or military mission where there was a loss of life. Perhaps you were the only survivor or one of a few survivors. While naturally relieved to be alive, you simultaneously may be mourning the deaths of others who were less fortunate. It is not uncommon for survivors to feel guilty about being spared from 2-8

FM 3-05.70 death while others were not. This feeling, when used in a positive way, has encouraged people to try harder to survive with the belief they were allowed to live for some greater purpose in life. Sometimes, survivors tried to stay alive so that they could carry on the work of those killed. Whatever reason you give yourself, do not let guilt feelings prevent you from living. The living who abandon their chance to survive accomplish nothing. Such an act would be the greatest tragedy. PREPARING YOURSELF 2-24. Your mission in a survival situation is to stay alive. The assortment of thoughts and emotions you will experience in a survival situation can work for you, or they can work to your downfall. Fear, anxiety, anger, frustration, guilt, depression, and loneliness are all possible reactions to the many stressors common to survival. These reactions, when controlled in a healthy way, help to increase your likelihood of surviving. They prompt you to pay more attention in training, to fight back when scared, to take actions that ensure sustenance and security, to keep faith with your fellow team members, and to strive against large odds. When you cannot control these reactions in

to pay more attention in training, to fight back when scared, to take actions that ensure sustenance and security, to keep faith with your fellow team members, and to strive against large odds. When you cannot control these reactions in a healthy way, they can bring you to a standstill. Instead of rallying your internal resources, you listen to your internal fears. These fears will cause you to experience psychological defeat long before you physically succumb. Remember, survival is natural to everyone; being unexpectedly thrust into the life-or-death struggle of survival is not. Do not be afraid of your “natural reactions to this unnatural situation.” Prepare yourself to rule over these reactions so they serve your ultimate interest—staying alive with honor and dignity. 2-25. Being prepared involves knowing that your reactions in a survival setting are productive, not destructive. The challenge of survival has produced countless examples of heroism, courage, and self-sacrifice. These are the qualities a survival situation can bring out in you if you have prepared yourself. Below are a few tips to help prepare yourself psychologically for survival. Through studying this manual and attending survival training you can develop the “survival attitude.” 2-9

FM 3-05.70 KNOW YOURSELF 2-26. You should take the time through training, family, and friends to discover who you are on the inside. Strengthen your stronger qualities and develop the areas that you know are necessary to survive. ANTICIPATE FEARS 2-27. Don’t pretend that you will have no fears. Begin thinking about what would frighten you the most if forced to survive alone. Train in those areas of concern to you. The goal is not to eliminate the fear, but to build confidence in your ability to function despite your fears. BE REALISTIC 2-28. Don’t be afraid to make an honest appraisal of situations. See circumstances as they are, not as you want them to be. Keep your hopes and expectations within the estimate of the situation. When you go into a survival setting with unrealistic expectations, you may be laying the groundwork for bitter disappointment. Follow the adage, “Hope for the best, prepare for the worst.” It is much easier to adjust to pleasant surprises about your unexpected good fortunes than to be upset by your unexpected harsh circumstances. ADOPT A POSITIVE ATTITUDE 2-29. Learn to see the potential good in everything. Looking for the good not only boosts

easier to adjust to pleasant surprises about your unexpected good fortunes than to be upset by your unexpected harsh circumstances. ADOPT A POSITIVE ATTITUDE 2-29. Learn to see the potential good in everything. Looking for the good not only boosts morale, it also is excellent for exercising your imagination and creativity. REMIND YOURSELF WHAT IS AT STAKE 2-30. Failure to prepare yourself psychologically to cope with survival leads to reactions such as depression, carelessness, inattention, loss of confidence, poor decision making, and giving up before the body gives in. Remember that your life and the lives of others who depend on you are at stake. TRAIN 2-31. Through military training and life experiences, begin today to prepare yourself to cope with the rigors of survival. Demonstrating your skills in training will give you the confidence 2-10

FM 3-05.70 to call upon them should the need arise. Remember, the more realistic the training, the less overwhelming an actual survival setting will be. LEARN STRESS MANAGEMENT TECHNIQUES 2-32. People under stress have a potential to panic if they are not well-trained and not prepared psychologically to face whatever the circumstances may be. While you often cannot control the survival circumstances in which you find yourself, it is within your ability to control your response to those circumstances. Learning stress management techniques can significantly enhance your capability to remain calm and focused as you work to keep yourself and others alive. A few good techniques to develop include relaxation skills, time management skills, assertiveness skills, and cognitive restructuring skills (the ability to control how you view a situation). Remember, “the will to survive” can also be considered “the refusal to give up.” 2-11

Chapter 3 Survival Planning and Survival Kits A survival plan is dependent on three separate but intertwined parts to be successful: planning, preparation, and practice. Survival planning is nothing more than realizing something could happen that would put you in a survival situation and, with that in mind, taking steps to increase your chances of survival. It can happen to anyone, anywhere, anytime, so remember: failure to plan is a plan to fail. Plans are based on evasion and recovery (E&R) considerations and the availability of resupply or emergency bundles. Planning also entails looking at those E&R routes and knowing by memory the major geographical features in case your map and compass are lost. Chapter 4 Basic Survival Medicine Foremost among the many problems that can compromise your survival ability are medical problems resulting from unplanned events, such as a forced landing or crash, extreme climates, ground combat, evasion, and illnesses contracted in captivity. Many evaders and survivors have reported difficulty in treating injuries and illness due to the lack of training and medical supplies. For some, this led to capture or surrender. Survivors have related feelings of apathy and helplessness because they could not treat themselves in this environment. The ability to treat yourself increases your morale and aids in your survival and eventual return to friendly forces. One man with a fair amount of basic medical knowledge can make a difference in the lives of many. Without qualified medical personnel available, it is you who must know what to do to stay alive. During average daily exertion when the atmospheric temperature is 20 degrees Celsius (C) (68 degrees Fahrenheit [F]), the average adult loses and therefore requires 2 to 3 liters of water daily. Dehydration results from inadequate replacement of lost body fluids. It decreases your efficiency and, if you are injured, it increases your susceptibility to severe shock. Consider the following results of body fluid loss: • A 5-percent loss results in thirst, irritability, nausea, and weakness. • A 10-percent loss results in dizziness, headache, inability to walk, and a tingling sensation in the limbs. • A 15-percent loss results in dim vision, painful urination, swollen tongue, deafness, and a numb feeling in the skin. • A loss greater than 15 percent may result in death. 4-4. The most common signs and symptoms of dehydration are— • Dark urine with a very strong odor. • Low urine output. • Dark, sunken eyes. • Fatigue. • Emotional instability. • Loss of skin elasticity. • Delayed capillary refill in fingernail beds. • Trench line down center of tongue. • Thirst. (Last on the list because you are already 2-percent dehydrated by the time you crave fluids.) 4-5. You should replace the water as you lose it. Trying

You should replace the water as you lose it. Trying to make up a deficit is difficult in a survival situation, and thirst is not a sign of how much water you need. 4-6. Most people cannot comfortably drink more than 1 liter of water at a time. So, even when not thirsty, drink small amounts of water at regular intervals each hour to prevent dehydration. 4-7. If you are under physical and mental stress or subject to severe conditions, increase your water intake. Drink enough liquids to maintain a urine output of at least 0.5 liters every 24 hours. 4-2

FM 3-05.70 4-8. In any situation where food intake is low, drink 6 to 8 liters of water per day. In an extreme climate, especially an arid one, the average person can lose 2.5 to 3.5 liters of water per hour. In this type of climate, you should drink 8 to 12 ounces of water every 30 minutes. It is better to regulate water loss through work or rest cycles because overhydration can occur if water intake exceed 1 1/2 quarts per hour. Overhydration can cause low serum sodium levels resulting in cerebral and pulmonary edema, which can lead to death. 4-9. With the loss of water there is also a loss of electrolytes (body salts). The average diet can usually keep up with these losses but in an extreme situation or illness, additional sources need to be provided. You should maintain an intake of carbohydrates and other necessary electrolytes. 4-10. Of all the physical problems encountered in a survival situation, the loss of water is the most preventable.
